final_proof:
By Definition 1, an adjunction between $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ is given by a pair of covariant functors $F : \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ and $G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$, together with a natural isomorphism $\alpha: \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-, -) \to \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-, G-)$ between the two hom-bifunctors from $\mathbf D^{\mathrm{op}} \times \mathbf C$ to $\mathbf{Set}$.

A natural isomorphism to the category of sets is exactly a natural transformation whose components are isomorphisms in $\mathbf{Set}$. Since an isomorphism in the category of sets is precisely a bijection, the components of $\alpha$ form a family of bijections:
$$\alpha_{(D^\text{op}, C)} : \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD, C) \to \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D, GC)$$
indexed by objects $(D^\text{op}, C)$ in $\mathbf D^\text{op} \times \mathbf C$, or equivalently by objects $D$ in $\mathbf D$ and $C$ in $\mathbf C$.

By the definition of a natural transformation, for any morphism $(f^\text{op}, g)$ in the product category $\mathbf D^\text{op} \times \mathbf C$, where $f^\text{op}: D_1^\text{op} \to D_2^\text{op}$ in $\mathbf D^\text{op}$ (which corresponds to a morphism $f: D_2 \to D_1$ in $\mathbf D$) and $g: C_1 \to C_2$ in $\mathbf C$, the naturality square must commute. This means that:
$$\alpha_{(D_2^\text{op}, C_2)} \circ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^\text{op}, g) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^\text{op}, Gg) \circ \alpha_{(D_1^\text{op}, C_1)}$$

Let us determine the actions of the hom-bifunctors on the morphisms. 
The functor $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(F-, -)$ maps the morphism $(f^\text{op}, g)$ to the function:
$$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Ff^\text{op}, g): \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD_1, C_1) \to \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(FD_2, C_2)$$
defined by $h \mapsto g \circ h \circ Ff$. This is well-defined because $Ff: FD_2 \to FD_1$ and $g: C_1 \to C_2$, so $g \circ h \circ Ff$ is a morphism $FD_2 \to C_2$.

Similarly, the functor $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(-, G-)$ maps $(f^\text{op}, g)$ to the function:
$$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(f^\text{op}, Gg): \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D_1, GC_1) \to \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf D}(D_2, GC_2)$$
defined by $h \mapsto Gg \circ h \circ f$. This is well-defined because $f: D_2 \to D_1$ and $Gg: GC_1 \to GC_2$, so $Gg \circ h \circ f$ is a morphism $D_2 \to GC_2$.

These functions are exactly the mappings defined in Definition 2. Thus, the naturality condition of Definition 1 is identical to the commutative diagram (and its equational form) explicitly written out in Definition 2.

Since Definition 1 requires a natural isomorphism (a family of bijections satisfying naturality) between these specific bifunctors, and Definition 2 explicitly requires a family of bijections satisfying exactly the same naturality condition, the two definitions are mathematically equivalent.
$\blacksquare$
